claims.text: Directional solidification is proposed as the intervention for boride-based components.
Conventionally processed boride-based components have a coarse-grained structure with extensive continuous grain boundaries.
The grain boundaries in conventional boride-based components facilitate rapid aluminum diffusion.
Rapid aluminum diffusion through grain boundaries promotes interfacial degradation under hot-dip aluminum-plating conditions.
Directional solidification can significantly refine the grains of the boride phases.
Directional solidification can produce preferential grain orientation in the boride phases.
The resulting refined microstructure has controlled grain-boundary characteristics and reduced continuity and density of fast diffusion pathways.
High-angle grain boundaries serve as fast diffusion channels for aluminum.
Grain refinement minimizes intergranular connectivity and the associated high-angle grain boundaries.
Reducing fast grain-boundary diffusion pathways limits molten-aluminum penetration and reaction at vulnerable interfacial regions.
Limiting aluminum penetration and interfacial reaction slows corrosion.
Directionally solidified components will have a longer time before corrosion onset than conventionally processed coarse-grained components.
Directionally solidified components will exhibit less aluminum penetration than conventionally processed components.
Directional solidification will improve the service life of boride-based components relative to conventional processing.
The improvement is expected to remain effective during molten-aluminum exposure above 600 °C with thermal cycling.
Severe contaminants or processing defects may become dominant corrosion mechanisms and diminish the benefit.
The magnitude of the corrosion-resistance improvement likely depends on the degree of grain refinement and the grain-boundary characteristics.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis characterizes a coarse-grained structure as having extensive grain-boundary pathways, while asserting that reducing grain size decreases grain-boundary-path density and connectivity. Grain refinement ordinarily increases total grain-boundary area unless a separately demonstrated change in boundary type, texture, or connectivity offsets that effect.
